title: Tier 1: the nine numbers the Cat chain starts from
body_html:
Every finder in this lane runs the same chain: nine numbers make edges, edges make shapes, shapes make the Cat. This record is Tier 1 of that chain: the nine numbers.

The Sobel Gx kernel is [[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]. Read it as a sentence: the left column subtracts, the right column adds, the middle column looks away, and the middle row counts double. Gy is the same square turned on its side, asking "is the bottom brighter than the top?" Where the picture is flat the positives and negatives cancel to zero. Where brightness jumps - the outline of the Cat against the background - the numbers fire.

The demo draws the Cat test drawing on a 48-by-48 grid and runs the real 3-by-3 convolution in pure Python, no libraries. Peak response: 840. Edge pixels above threshold: 362. Tier 2 never sees the drawing - it only ever sees these 362 edge pixels.

title: Tier 2 inventory: making the Cat from shapes
body_html:
Before any detection runs, the Cat is built as an arrangement of Tier-2 shapes on a 48-by-48 test grid. The inventory: 2 triangles, 1 circles, 1 ellipses, 1 lines.

The map below is the exact test image the finder sees - # is drawn, . is background. Everything the finder knows about a Cat lives in this map.

Each shape is drawn filled (lines are drawn thick). Edges form exactly along the outlines, which is what the Tier-2 shape finders in the next record hunt for.

title: The Tier-2 shape finders that catch each part
body_html:
Tier 2 turns edge pixels into named shapes. Each part of the Cat gets a dedicated finder: circle-finder, ellipse-finder, line-finder, triangle-finder.

Each finder sweeps an outline template of its shape over a small search window around the part's expected pose and scores the overlap with the real edge map. A score of 1.0 would be a perfect outline; a part counts as found at 0.40 or better.

Live scores on the test drawing - every part found: head 0.643; ear left 0.714; ear right 0.714; body 0.689; tail 0.816.

title: The shape recipe - what the Cat is made of
body_html:
A cat is two triangles up, one round head, one ellipse body, one tail curve. Take the ears away and the "cat" collapses into a blob with a tail — the ears are the cat signature.

Measured off the test drawing: head: circle, radius 7, center (24,15). ear left: tri, spans x 16-23, y 2-10, center (19,7). ear right: tri, spans x 25-32, y 2-10, center (28,7). body: ellipse, 18x12, center (24,32). tail: line, from (31,33) to (39,25), center (35,29).

Proportions are part of the recipe, not decoration: parts run from about 132 px (ear left) to about 484 px (body) of bounding area. The finder expects roughly these sizes - a head the size of the body would break the arrangement gate in the next record.

title: The knowing-when rule - the decision that says "CAT FOUND"
body_html:
Knowing when the edges made the shape is a decision rule with two gates. Gate 1 - parts: every part's shape score must reach 0.40. Gate 2 - arrangement: every one of these checks must pass: 1. left ear sits above the head; 2. right ear sits above the head; 3. body hangs below the head; 4. head and body vertically stacked; 5. tail trails right of the body.

The demo runs the rule two ways. On the test Cat: FOUND, weakest part 0.643 (margin 0.243 above threshold). With the ear left erased: NOT FOUND - the rule genuinely depends on the parts.

Across the other twelve test drawings, this finder's full rule also fires on: Human face, Tree, House, Flower. Where it fires on a cousin - the cat finder also fires on the dog drawing - that is measured, not hidden: simple shape recipes overlap, and telling close cousins apart needs more evidence than outlines alone. The rule as built is reported exactly as measured.

title: The full chain, executed - nine numbers to Cat
body_html:
Here is the whole chain in one program. Tier 1 runs the nine numbers (the Sobel pair) over the drawing and keeps the edge pixels. Tier 2 runs one shape finder per part. Tier 3 applies the knowing-when rule - part scores plus arrangement checks - and prints its verdict.

The program below is the working version of this database (find-cat.py): pure Python, no libraries, no numpy. The output beneath it is the real captured stdout from the build - not a mock.

Demonstrated on synthetic test shapes. This proves the chain executes end to end on clean drawings. It does not claim detection on real photographs.

title: The finder holds - shifted, noisy, still found
body_html:
Robustness check, executed: shift the whole Cat by (+3, -2) pixels and sprinkle 40 random bright noise pixels across the grid - dirt on the lens. The finder still says FOUND.

Scores move a little (weakest part 0.636) but every part stays above 0.40 and every arrangement check passes.

What this proves: the rule tolerates small shifts and dirt. What it does not prove: rotation, occlusion, or photographs - those are outside the test.

title: Honest limits - what is proven and what is not
body_html:
Proven, by execution: on clean 48-by-48 synthetic drawings, the chain nine-numbers to edges to shapes to Cat runs end to end in pure Python, and the knowing-when rule (part scores at 0.40 plus arrangement checks) fires FOUND on the Cat - and, measured honestly, also on Human face, Tree, House, Flower.

Not proven: real photographs, hand-drawn variants, rotated or occluded cats, lighting changes, or anything outside the test grid. Nothing in this database was ever run on a camera image, and nothing here claims otherwise.

Noise curve, executed (random bright pixels added): 0 noise px: 5/5 parts, 5/5 checks -> FOUND 40 noise px: 5/5 parts, 5/5 checks -> FOUND 120 noise px: 5/5 parts, 5/5 checks -> FOUND 300 noise px: 5/5 parts, 5/5 checks -> FOUND.
